💸📉 YOUR “FAIR” PRICE MIGHT BE KILLING YOUR GROWTH
 
One Price for Everyone? That’s the Fastest Way to Lose Customers
 
Category: FINANCIAL WISDOM
 
I’ve watched entrepreneurs leave thousands of dollars on the table — for one simple reason.
 
They assumed every customer, in every country, values money the same way.
 
They don’t.
 
A price that feels “cheap” in New York can feel impossible in Lagos. A price that feels “premium” in London might actually reduce trust in Jakarta.
 
That’s the quiet truth most founders miss — and it’s costing you growth.
 
💡 Pricing isn’t math. It’s emotion, timing, and local reality.
 
Right now, pressure is everywhere. Acquisition costs are up. Demand is shifting. Investors are pushing for faster revenue. So founders react — they slash prices globally… or force one number onto the whole world.
 
Both are dangerous.
 
Ignoring local purchasing power is like building a skyscraper on sand. It looks solid — until the foundation shifts. ⚠️
 
💡 I consulted a SaaS founder who learned this the hard way. He launched globally at $19/$29/$49. Traffic was strong. Interest was high. But conversions in emerging markets? Almost zero.
 
Instead of spending more on ads, he changed one thing. He tested regional pricing.
 
💰 Wealthy markets → kept premium.
🌍 Emerging markets → $3/$7/$12 tiers.
 
The result? Revenue increased across every region. The mid-tier option became the bestseller everywhere. Customers finally felt the price matched their reality.
 
Data from ProfitWell backs this up — smart regional pricing can lift conversions by nearly 30%.
 
🧠 The entrepreneurs winning globally aren’t always cheaper. They’re simply more relevant.
 
 
 
✅ ACTIONABLE STEPS 
 
1️⃣ Map purchasing power before setting global pricing.

2️⃣ Test at least 3 price points within 30 days.

3️⃣ Track conversions per country — never average them.

4️⃣ Build a strong mid-tier — most people avoid extremes.

5️⃣ Ask local users directly: “Does this feel fair to you?”

6️⃣ Chase sustainable profit — not vanity revenue screenshots.
 
 
 
📊 POLL 

Which pricing mistake hurts you most?
 
🔘 One global price for everyone
🔘 Pricing too low out of fear
🔘 Ignoring local psychology
🔘 Copying competitors blindly
 
 
 
🚨 COMMON MYSTAKES

⚠️ You’re pricing globally because others do it — not because your customers need it.
 
⚠️ Too-low pricing can destroy trust faster than high pricing.
 
⚠️ If your pricing is based on assumptions instead of testing — cash burn is inevitable.
 
The bottom line: Sustainable growth doesn’t come from charging everyone the same. It comes from understanding how different people experience value. 

Adapt without losing profitability. That’s the sweet spot — and it’s where the winners play.
 
✍️ Is your pricing global or local? Has a price change ever unlocked massive growth? Let’s discuss in the comments — I’d love to hear your story.

🚀 Introducing DailyMart POS – A Point of Sale (POS) & Management Web Application

I'm excited to share a demo of DailyMart POS, a modern and responsive POS web application developed as part of my coursework at Institute of Computer Engineering Technology (iCET).

The goal of this project was to build a practical system that simplifies everyday operations for retail stores and cafés by bringing product management, order handling, customer management, and checkout into one application.

✨ 🌟 Key Features

🛍️ 1. Point of Sale & Product Management

🔍 Browse and search products.
➕ Add new products with names, categories, descriptions, prices, and images.
🛒 Dynamic product selection and order summaries.
🍽️ Dine-In and Takeaway order options.
🧮 Automatic subtotal, 8% tax, and grand total calculations.

💳 2. Checkout & Payment

💵 Cash and card payment selection.
💰 Quick cash denomination shortcuts.
🧾 Real-time change and balance calculations.
✅ Payment success confirmation with transaction summary.

📦 3. Order Management

📋 View order history with order IDs, dates, payment details, and totals.
🔎 View individual order details.
✏️ Edit and delete orders.
📄 Pagination for managing order records.

👥 4. Customer Management

➕ Add, view, edit, and delete customer records.
🆔 Automatically generated customer IDs.
⭐ Active and VIP customer status indicators.
📊 Customer details and spending information.
📄 Pagination for customer records.

🛡️ 5. Form Validation & Error Handling

Implemented validation checks in different parts of the application to improve data accuracy and prevent incomplete operations.

📝 Product Validation – AddProduct.jsx:

Checks required fields (product name, category, and price) and validates that the price can be converted into a numeric value using Number() and Number.isNaN().

🛒 Order Validation – Receipt.jsx:

Prevents checkout when the order is empty and displays a warning notification when users attempt to charge without adding products.

💳 Payment Validation – ChargePopUp.jsx:

Checks whether the cash received field is empty and prevents completing a cash sale when the amount received is less than the total bill.

👤 Customer Validation – CustomerManagement.jsx:

Prevents adding or updating customer records when the customer name is blank. Phone number and email are optional.

🔔 User Feedback: Integrated Sonner toast notifications to display validation warnings and provide immediate feedback.

🛠️💻 Technologies & Tools Used

⚛️ React 19 – Component-based architecture and interactive UI development.
🟨JavaScript (ES6+) – Application logic, event handling, array methods, and data manipulation.
🧩JSX – Writing UI structures within React components.
🔄React Hooks (useState, useEffect) – State management and handling side effects.
🎨Tailwind CSS v4 – Responsive layouts and modern UI styling.
⚡Vite 8 – Development server and production build tooling.
🔔Sonner – Toast notifications and validation feedback.
🧱Uiverse.io – Animated UI components and button interactions.
🔤Google Fonts (Plus Jakarta Sans) – Typography.
🌐HTML5 & CSS3 – Application structure and custom styling.
💾Local Storage API – Retaining the order number counter between page refreshes.
🔍ESLint & npm – Code linting and dependency management.
🐙Git & GitHub – Source code management and version control.

📚💡 What I Learned

Building Pay Nest gave me valuable hands-on experience with:

⚛️ React component architecture and reusable components.
🔗 Passing data between components using props.
🔄 Managing state and sharing data between components.
🖱️ Handling events and user interactions.
📋 Rendering and managing dynamic lists using .map(), .filter(), and .slice().
🛡️ Implementing form validation and conditional rendering.
💾 Working with browser Local Storage.
📝 Building CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete).
📄 Creating pagination functionality.
💳 Implementing checkout workflows and payment calculations.
📱 Designing responsive user interfaces with Tailwind CSS.

This project has been a great learning experience, helping me connect theoretical concepts with practical frontend development.

I'm continuously learning, building, and improving my skills through hands-on projects. 🚀

This year I taught React at the school I was still a student at.

From January to June 2026, I taught 20+ grade 10 and 11 students in the software engineering program (RPL) at SMK Letris Indonesia 2. A month before my teaching ended, I graduated from the same school.

We covered modern JavaScript, React components, state, and how real teams actually build and ship.

What it taught me:

1. If you really understand it, you can find the analogy.
When I truly understood a concept, I could explain it with an analogy that fit my students' world. When I couldn't, I didn't understand it well enough yet.

2. Students copy your habits, not your slides.
So I started writing code the way I'd want it reviewed.

3. Teaching made me a better developer.
You don't really understand a concept until someone asks "but why?" five times in a row.

Today I build production software as a Full Stack Developer at Konksi, and I still use what that class taught me every time I write docs for my team.

🏗️ Could Modular Construction Change the Way Southeast Asia Builds Data Centers?

For years, traditional on-site construction has been the foundation of data center development.

But as project schedules become increasingly demanding, is the industry approaching a turning point?

🇲🇾 In Johor, Malaysia, EPG Modular Data Center has reached a significant milestone with its new manufacturing facility in Senai Airport City.

Representing an investment of approximately US$120 million, the facility will support the production of prefabricated modular data center infrastructure.

It’s an interesting development for the industry.

Rather than installing and assembling everything on-site, more critical infrastructure could be manufactured, assembled and tested in controlled factory environments before delivery.

The potential advantages?

✅ More predictable manufacturing quality.

✅ Reduced on-site installation activities.

✅ Opportunities for parallel construction and manufacturing.

✅ Greater standardisation across multiple projects.

✅ Potential improvements in project delivery schedules.

But modular construction also introduces challenges.

Transport logistics, interface coordination, factory acceptance testing, installation tolerances and integration with site infrastructure all require careful management.

And a factory-tested module is not necessarily a fully commissioned system once installed.

💬 LET’S START A DISCUSSION

If you were responsible for delivering a new 100 MW data center in Southeast Asia, which approach would you prefer?

A: Traditional on-site construction.

B: Fully modular and prefabricated systems.

C: A hybrid approach combining both.

And more importantly, WHY?

We’d love to hear from project managers, engineers, contractors, QA/QC specialists, commissioning teams and developers with real project experience.

Nvidia halts AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries — buyers found out from Dell and Supermicro that their orders won't ship

Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Dell and Supermicro, which package Nvidia's chips into servers, have told buyers in the four countries that Nvidia will not allow their orders to be shipped.

There was no announcement. The news reached the region's data-center builders the way a cancellation reaches a passenger: at the counter, at the last moment. The orders exist. The buildings are rising. The servers are not coming.

The trigger is Washington's new export rule, in force since November 19. The Commerce Department now requires a license for advanced-chip shipments to the four countries — and for overseas data centers that supply significant computing power to companies based in China. The target is the back door: Chinese developers renting Nvidia power in data centers abroad that they could not import at home. Reuters reported the same day that the restrictions could delay the next flagship models from China's Z.AI and Moonshot AI, whose development cycles could double if that overseas computing is cut off.

The four countries are where the rule lands. Malaysia and Singapore sit at the center of Southeast Asia's data-center boom, much of it built to serve exactly that demand. Fitch Ratings warned on Thursday that data-center investment across Asia-Pacific will slow and turn more selective, that the operators renting out GPU capacity face the greatest pressure, and that capital will move toward projects whose chip supply is secure.

How long the halt lasts, nobody has said: the Financial Times reports that Nvidia and its partners are still working out how to comply. Nvidia, Dell and Supermicro did not respond to requests for comment.

Story in development: the halt is reported by the Financial Times, has not been confirmed by the companies involved, and its duration is unknown.

New US Export Rules on AI Chips Could Slow Chinese Data Centre Investment in Southeast Asia

The US Bureau of Industry and Security announced new export restrictions on November 19 that tighten access to advanced AI chips. The rules close a workaround Chinese technology companies used to reach advanced US chips through data centres built or leased outside China, and they affect data centre growth across Southeast Asia.

• Certain AI chip shipments to data centres in Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, plus Brazil, now require export licences because of diversion risks.
• New AI data centre investments by Chinese hyperscalers could face delays, and existing facilities supporting advanced AI training workloads could be affected.
• Conventional cloud computing and less compute-intensive applications are expected to be less affected.
• The restrictions are likely to limit Chinese hyperscalers' advanced AI training capacity through 2027, and wider adoption of domestic chips could ease constraints from 2028.
• Malaysia remains one of Southeast Asia's more attractive data centre growth markets, supported by its proximity to Singapore and relatively developed infrastructure.
• Data centre construction costs in Southeast Asia run roughly 25% to 30% higher than in China, where an established supply chain and mature contractor ecosystem give a cost advantage.
• Project timelines in Southeast Asia typically run 12 to 15 months, compared with six to nine months in China.
• Singapore remains a key regional connectivity hub but faces high land and operating costs, limited space and restrictive capacity allocations.
• Selective regional expansion by US hyperscalers is expected to continue, with no substantial relocation of their AI computing infrastructure from the United States to Southeast Asia.
• Data centre exposure makes up about 3% to 5% of Singapore banks' total loans, versus 1% to 2% for most global peers.
• Slower financing demand could pull FY2027 loan growth in Singapore toward the mid-single-digit range, and a shift to lower-yielding lending segments could pressure margins. Fee income impact is expected to stay limited, and asset quality risks look manageable.
• Long-term leases of 10 to 15 years and substantial early termination penalties reduce the immediate impact on data centre developers.

Export controls on advanced chips are now shaping where and how fast AI data centre capacity gets built across Southeast Asia.

Nvidia has told its server partners to stop shipping AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries, in the sharpest move yet to cut off China's access to its most advanced chips. The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Dell and Supermicro have told customers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia will not allow orders to be shipped, citing three people familiar with the matter.

The four countries had become the main workaround for Chinese AI developers barred from buying Nvidia chips directly: instead of buying the hardware, they rented computing power from Southeast Asian cloud firms running Nvidia-powered servers. Last week the US Commerce Department moved to close that loophole, requiring cloud providers to win a separate licence within 90 days by proving no sanctioned entity is among their end users, and requiring data centres already leasing large amounts of compute to Chinese firms to get US approval to keep operating.

The stakes are large on both sides. Nvidia booked $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary last year, up 72% year on year, though some of that is Taiwan and China revenue routed through Singapore. At the same time, the money behind the region's data-centre boom is stalling: Bloomberg reported banks including Citigroup, Standard Chartered, DBS, OCBC and UOB are reviewing loans tied to ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, with a $6.6 billion upsized loan for Bain Capital's Bridge Data Centres delayed and about $500 million in funding for ByteDance supplier Aolani suspended.

It is not yet clear whether the halt is temporary while Nvidia works out how to comply with the new US rules, or a longer freeze. What is clear is that the chip war has moved from blocking direct sales to policing the cloud itself — and Southeast Asia's data-centre boom, built largely on Chinese demand, is now caught in the middle.

Nvidia’s ASEAN Server Freeze: A Reality Check for Malaysia’s Data Center Boom

Reports that Nvidia has instructed OEM partners including Dell and Supermicro to halt AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia mark a pivotal turning point for Southeast Asia’s digital infrastructure market.

Triggered by tightened U.S. Commerce Department export licensing rules aimed at closing the "cloud loophole" and curbing alleged chip diversion, this freeze will not derail Malaysia’s data center (DC) trajectory but it will fundamentally reshape DC investment projects.

Here is how this development impacts Malaysia’s DC investment landscape:
1. Immediate Deployment Bottlenecks & Stranded CapEx
Blocking high-end systems like Grace Blackwell racks pending export licenses creates an immediate commissioning gap for AI-ready facilities in Johor and Cyberjaya. A powered shell without GPUs cannot generate AI compute revenue, pushing back project timelines and delaying returns on upfront capital expenditure.
2. Tighter Credit & Project Financing
With approved DC investments in Malaysia exceeding RM385 billion, debt financing is critical to execution. Regional banks are already freezing credit lines for AI projects tied to Chinese off-takers due to counterparty and regulatory risks. Expect lenders to enforce stricter compliance covenants before disbursing funds to debt-heavy colocation developers.
3. A Divided Market: Hyperscalers vs. Neoclouds
The impact will hit market segments unevenly:
• High Exposure: Third-party AI cloud providers ("neoclouds") and colocation operators reliant on Chinese tech demand face severe business-model disruption, as new rules require licensing even for remote compute leasing to Chinese-headquartered firms.
• Resilient Core: U.S. hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Oracle) building enterprise and sovereign cloud regions have established compliance architectures and are far better positioned to secure U.S. export approvals once licensing workflows stabilize.
4. Utility & Supply Chain Spillovers
Delayed server deliveries mean actual power draw (load ramp-up) will lag behind initial grid connection schedules. While long-term infrastructure demand remains intact, near-term utilization for dedicated power, gas, and water infrastructure alongside mechanical, electrical, and plumbing contractors will see a measurable slowdown.

This is a compliance reset, not a permanent exit. Malaysia’s fundamentals (land, power capacity, and regional connectivity) remain compelling. However, the era of "open-hub" AI deployment is over. Moving forward, attracting institutional capital into Malaysia’s DC sector will hinge on strict Know-Your-Customer (KYC) governance, transparent supply chains, and verifiable end-user auditing.

AI compute access is becoming an export-control issue—even when the GPUs never cross a border.

A US Commerce Department rule effective 19 November 2026 adds licensing controls for certain advanced-computing items destined for overseas data centres that provide more than 12 million aggregate TPP of compute to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination. The rule also covers linked data centres and requires due diligence on direct and indirect ownership or control.

Separately, it adds licensing requirements for specified advanced semiconductor exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, subject to defined exceptions.

The timing matters. In a 26 November report, Reuters said Chinese AI developers Z.AI and Moonshot may face delays to planned model releases and longer development cycles if overseas compute access is restricted. Those company-specific forecasts are attributed to people familiar with the matter—not formal statements from the companies.

The business shift is clear: compute procurement is no longer only a question of GPU availability, price, power and latency. End-user identity, ultimate-parent ownership, remote access, linked facilities and downstream use are becoming part of the compliance architecture.

For data-centre operators, cloud providers and AI buyers, the practical checks are:
• Verify the contracting customer and ultimate parent.
• Map who can remotely access the compute and for whose benefit.
• Review linked data-centre arrangements and changes in end use.
• Build export-control screening and recordkeeping into onboarding and renewals.

A cloud contract can cross borders without a single server moving. Compliance has to follow the compute.

If your business rents advanced AI compute, are end-user and ownership checks built into procurement?

US chip controls are becoming a structural constraint on Asia’s data-center investment cycle—not merely a compliance issue.

Fitch Ratings expects investment across Asia-Pacific to slow and become more selective as new US licensing requirements affect chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, as well as overseas facilities serving Chinese customers.

Why this matters

The AI infrastructure boom is increasingly dependent on two scarce inputs: advanced semiconductors and eligible, creditworthy demand.

The new rules may:

Redirect capital toward projects with secure chip access and diversified customers.
Increase the gap between physical data-center owners and highly leveraged “neocloud” operators.
Delay revenue generation for nearly completed facilities awaiting chips or customer approvals.
Tighten lending standards as banks reassess supply-chain and regulatory exposure.
Pressure China-focused operators to reduce prices, use less advanced hardware or extend the life of existing Nvidia systems.

Neocloud providers face particular vulnerability because their business model depends on keeping expensive GPUs highly utilized. Any disruption to Chinese demand or hardware upgrades can quickly reduce margins and debt-servicing capacity.

Investment implications

The market should distinguish between:

Data-center landlords with contracted, diversified demand.
Compute providers with concentrated Chinese exposure.
Developers relying on uncertain chip allocations or aggressive leverage.

The most resilient projects will combine secured semiconductor supply, diversified customers, strong power access and conservative financing. AI demand remains powerful, but capital allocation will increasingly depend on geopolitical eligibility—not only expected compute demand.

Key takeaway

The next phase of the AI infrastructure cycle will reward operational resilience and balance-sheet quality. Investors should stress-test utilization, customer concentration, chip replacement cycles and regulatory eligibility before treating data-center growth forecasts as bankable.

What do you think: will chip controls slow AI investment, or simply redirect it toward more compliant and diversified markets?

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO less than two weeks after resigning. The board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate him and concluded his return poses no national security risk. The investigation will continue and Huang is due to be interviewed by House committees on 1 December and testify publicly to the Senate Banking Committee on 3 December. Separately, the Financial Times reports that Nvidia has told partners including Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers with its AI chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. It follows new US licensing rules and the blacklisting of Megaspeed, the Singapore firm linked to the allegations involving Huang. It's unclear whether the halt is temporary.

Anthropic's shares have fallen below their IPO price less than a week after listing. The stock opened at $111.50 and closed its first day at $97.17, then dropped under the $83 offer price on Tuesday. It closed Wednesday at $82.79, valuing the company at around $1.1 trillion, amid a wider fall in AI and chip stocks.

Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, which can review, fix and approve code changes. The beta, announced on Monday, combines three agents: one that reviews pull requests, one that fixes them and one that can approve routine changes if a team's policy allows it. It's available to Team and Enterprise customers with code on GitHub, and developers can try it with a new /ship command in Claude Code.

Amazon has agreed to buy the technology behind startup Decart for a reported $7.5 billion. "Can an Indonesian actually own property in Dubai?"

I get this question a lot from Indonesian families, both in Jakarta and in Singapore. Short answer: yes, outright.

A few things people are surprised by:

• Foreigners can buy freehold in Dubai's designated freehold areas, which cover most of the places people actually want to live or rent out.
• You don't need to live in the UAE or hold residency to buy.
• The title deed is issued by the Dubai Land Department, in your own name or a company's.
• When you buy off-plan, your payments go into a regulated escrow account, not straight to the developer.
• Abu Dhabi has opened up too. Foreigners can now own freehold in its investment zones.

The bigger questions are usually how to hold it (personal name, company or family structure) and how it passes to the next generation. That's where a bit of planning up front saves a lot later.

Curious what others have found. What surprised you most when you first looked at buying abroad?

【Current News】 Trump Says He Got Jensen Huang Back at Nvidia as the US Adds Megaspeed to Its Entity List

On Nov. 17, Nvidia's board said it did not intend to bring Jensen Huang back. On Nov. 23, the company announced that the board had voted unanimously to do so, 11 days after he resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman US officials suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. China has denied she is a spy. The board said input from senior levels of the US government left it confident that his return posed no national security risk.

Trump told CNBC on Nov. 23 that he had spoken to the board and convinced it to reinstate Huang. He said the previous week's selloff in tech stocks probably played a part, though the long term mattered more. Huang told a different story. At his first meeting with all staff on Nov. 24, he told employees it was completely untrue that he had been reinstated only at Trump's request, The New York Times reported. Nvidia's stock jumped 31% on Nov. 23, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, then gave back 5.9% the next day.

Lawmakers in both parties pushed back. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called the decision indefensible and promised an investigation. Senator Elizabeth Warren wants to know what input the administration gave and who gave it. Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican who chairs the Senate intelligence committee, said Huang's return did not resolve the Megaspeed controversy.

Megaspeed is where the story reaches Asia's supply chains. The Singapore data center developer was an Nvidia customer, and Alice Huang is a former executive. After investigating for almost two years whether Megaspeed helped Nvidia chips reach companies in China, the Commerce Department on Nov. 23 filed a final rule adding seven companies in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to the Entity List, including Megaspeed and Speedmatrix, effective that day. Any export, reexport or transfer within a country involving them now needs a license for all items subject to US export rules, and applications will be reviewed with a presumption of denial. Shipments already under way when it took effect have 30 days to be completed.

A separate rule has applied since Nov. 19. Certain advanced AI chips and servers now need a license to be exported or reexported to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, or transferred within those countries.

Huang is due for a private interview with three House committees on Dec. 1, and the Senate Banking Committee plans to hear his public testimony on Dec. 3. After Democrats take control in January, Jeffries is expected to become Speaker and Warren is set to chair the Banking Committee.

Unlike conventional green loans, sustainability-linked loans offer borrowers greater flexibility, with financial incentives tied to achieving agreed performance targets. The guidance helps banks and building owners identify improvements, assess their costs and benefits, and translate them into measurable outcomes from energy and emissions reductions to water efficiency and waste management.

This builds on GBPN’s wider work through the Green Finance Accelerator, which brings together financial institutions, policymakers and building-sector stakeholders to strengthen Indonesia’s green building finance market. The goal is to make sustainable building improvements easier to finance, implement and scale.

🔹Current gap and core barriers
With only 1.5 GW of installed solar capacity at the end of 2025, Indonesia faces structural frictions across its policy framework. Administratively set ceiling tariffs fail to reflect falling solar costs, land acquisition can take up to 40 months before construction starts, corporate buyers have limited routes to procure new clean power, rooftop solar lost its export credit incentive in 2024, and standalone battery storage lacks a dedicated regulatory framework.

🔹Key reform priorities
The report proposes six targeted fixes that preserve state utility PLN’s central role in the power system:

- Replace fixed ceiling tariffs with competitive reverse auctions to enable transparent price discovery.
- Centralise land preparation with standardised leasing options to de-risk project siting and shorten development cycles.
- Introduce virtual power purchase agreements (VPPAs) to unlock up to 12 GW of new solar capacity driven by corporate demand.
- Reinstate fair net billing for rooftop solar with grid safeguards, estimated to save the state IDR 1.9 trillion by 2030.
- Establish a clear remuneration framework for battery storage to support grid flexibility and firm solar supply.
- Streamline procurement through a dedicated agency working alongside PLN to standardise contracts and tender processes.

SNEC's Insights

1️⃣ For emerging solar markets, administrative efficiency and policy predictability matter more than raw resource potential. Governance bottlenecks typically slow deployment long before technology or cost become limiting factors.
2️⃣ VPPAs are a pragmatic middle path for markets without full power sector liberalisation. They channel corporate decarbonisation capital into new solar capacity while preserving utility revenue and grid control.
3️⃣ Pre-cleared, tender-ready sites are a high-impact, low-profile lever. Resolving land and grid access before auctions reduces developer risk far more effectively than incremental tariff incentives.

🔹Bottom line: 
The upcoming revision of Indonesia’s national electricity plan is a critical window to align regulation with its 100 GWp ambition. With targeted governance reforms, solar can become a core pillar of Indonesia’s energy security, industrial competitiveness and decarbonisation.

Emerging markets will drive the next wave of storage growth, but low export prices alone no longer win deals.

In recent conversations with storage integrators and an international developer in China, a clear geographic shift stood out. As mature markets moderate, commercial teams are focusing heavily on new growth pockets across Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East and Africa.

Three demand signals stand out right now. Based on InfoLink data, Chile is projected to more than double its annual storage additions from 16.6 GWh in 2026 to 36.6 GWh in 2027. In the Philippines, all new variable renewable energy projects with a capacity of 10 MW or more must now pair storage equivalent to at least 20 percent of installed capacity. Meanwhile, South Africa is advancing standalone storage tenders, while Egypt has cleared PPA financing for a 200 MWh project.

Yet winning these projects requires clearing three hardening barriers.

First, India ties viability gap funding to higher local value addition, echoing what I saw on the ground at REI last month. Second, Indonesia enforces local content rules that trace origin all the way back to battery cells and cathode materials, where only a handful of Chinese suppliers currently operate overseas cathode capacity. Third, Japan will require JC-STAR 1 cybersecurity certification for PCS and EMS on new grid connections from April 2027.

My read: 2027 emerging market winners will be defined by local compliance and grid certification, not export hardware pricing.

🔹Current gap and core barriers

With only 1.5 GW of installed solar capacity at the end of 2025, Indonesia faces structural frictions across its policy framework. Administratively set ceiling tariffs fail to reflect falling solar costs, land acquisition can take up to 40 months before construction starts, corporate buyers have limited routes to procure new clean power, rooftop solar lost its export credit incentive in 2024, and standalone battery storage lacks a dedicated regulatory framework.

🔹Key reform priorities

The report proposes six targeted fixes that preserve state utility PLN’s central role in the power system:

- Replace fixed ceiling tariffs with competitive reverse auctions to enable transparent price discovery.
- Centralise land preparation with standardised leasing options to de-risk project siting and shorten development cycles.
- Introduce virtual power purchase agreements (VPPAs) to unlock up to 12 GW of new solar capacity driven by corporate demand.
- Reinstate fair net billing for rooftop solar with grid safeguards, estimated to save the state IDR 1.9 trillion by 2030.
- Establish a clear remuneration framework for battery storage to support grid flexibility and firm solar supply.
- Streamline procurement through a dedicated agency working alongside PLN to standardise contracts and tender processes.

SNEC's Insights

1️⃣ For emerging solar markets, administrative efficiency and policy predictability matter more than raw resource potential. Governance bottlenecks typically slow deployment long before technology or cost become limiting factors.

2️⃣ VPPAs are a pragmatic middle path for markets without full power sector liberalisation. They channel corporate decarbonisation capital into new solar capacity while preserving utility revenue and grid control.

3️⃣ Pre-cleared, tender-ready sites are a high-impact, low-profile lever. Resolving land and grid access before auctions reduces developer risk far more effectively than incremental tariff incentives.

🔹Bottom line: 
The upcoming revision of Indonesia’s national electricity plan is a critical window to align regulation with its 100 GWp ambition. With targeted governance reforms, solar can become a core pillar of Indonesia’s energy security, industrial competitiveness and decarbonisation.

Introducing CAS (Coverage Analysis System) v1.1 — Beyond Coverage, Towards Resilience.
As a CNS engineer, I have always been interested in how technology can help us better understand the performance, coverage, and limitations of aviation infrastructure.
In an archipelagic country like Indonesia, with its complex terrain and geographical challenges, understanding the actual coverage of navigation, communication, and surveillance facilities is an important part of infrastructure planning and assessment.
This inspired me to develop CAS (Coverage Analysis System), an engineering tool that integrates terrain data, facility parameters, propagation models, and aeronautical information into a single geospatial analysis platform.
The current version, CAS v1.1, includes:
📡 Radar and ADS-B coverage analysis.
✈️ DME coverage and DME/DME RNAV availability analysis.
📶 VHF air-ground communication coverage using ITU-R propagation models.
🏔️ Terrain profile and Line-of-Sight (LOS) analysis using 30-meter Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data.
🌐 Multi-flight-level coverage, overlap, and blank spot analysis.
🗺️ ATS route, waypoint, and FIR boundary integration.
CAS is designed not only to visualize coverage but also to help engineers better understand the factors that influence infrastructure performance.
Looking ahead, I would like to explore further developments in DME/DME redundancy, critical DME identification, infrastructure outage simulation, and GNSS contingency assessment.
CAS remains an engineering research and development tool, with further validation required before operational application.
There is still much to learn and improve. I welcome discussions, feedback, and knowledge sharing with fellow CNS engineers, researchers, and aviation professionals.

During a recent field trip to Indonesia, I saw a track maintenance team using standard handheld angle grinders to cut heavy steel rails. 🛠️🚆
While versatile on standard metal, cutting heavy rail steel (like U71Mn or R260) with un-clamped handheld tools raises a vital technical question: How do we maintain structural integrity and safety under extreme friction?

Cutting rails isn't just about speed—it’s about preserving rail end quality for post-welding and protecting the operator. 3 critical factors to consider:
1️⃣ Lateral Impact Resistance: Handheld cutting generates severe lateral wobble. Multi-layer high-tensile fiberglass mesh isn't optional—it’s the core safety net.
2️⃣Cool Cutting & Thermal Control: Self-sharpening grains (like ceramic alumina) prevent excessive heat buildup, eliminating micro-cracking and heat-affected zones (HAZ).
3️⃣High Cut-Yield Speed: Completing a single heavy rail cut in ~60 seconds minimizes track possession time and operator fatigue.

Equipment realities vary by market, but rail safety compliance remains universal.
❓To the railway engineers, track supervisors, and MRO distributors in my network:
From your perspective as a rail industry professional—what truly makes a rail cutting disc a "good product"? Is it pure cutting speed, safety margins, or cost per cut?
I’d love to read your field insights in the comments! 👇

🏗️ Could Modular Construction Change the Way Southeast Asia Builds Data Centers?

For years, traditional on-site construction has been the foundation of data center development.

But as project schedules become increasingly demanding, is the industry approaching a turning point?

🇲🇾 In Johor, Malaysia, EPG Modular Data Center has reached a significant milestone with its new manufacturing facility in Senai Airport City.

Representing an investment of approximately US$120 million, the facility will support the production of prefabricated modular data center infrastructure.

It’s an interesting development for the industry.

Rather than installing and assembling everything on-site, more critical infrastructure could be manufactured, assembled and tested in controlled factory environments before delivery.

The potential advantages?

✅ More predictable manufacturing quality.

✅ Reduced on-site installation activities.

✅ Opportunities for parallel construction and manufacturing.

✅ Greater standardisation across multiple projects.

✅ Potential improvements in project delivery schedules.

But modular construction also introduces challenges.

Transport logistics, interface coordination, factory acceptance testing, installation tolerances and integration with site infrastructure all require careful management.

And a factory-tested module is not necessarily a fully commissioned system once installed.

💬 LET’S START A DISCUSSION

If you were responsible for delivering a new 100 MW data center in Southeast Asia, which approach would you prefer?

A: Traditional on-site construction.

B: Fully modular and prefabricated systems.

C: A hybrid approach combining both.

And more importantly, WHY?

The United States just proposed tariffs on 14 economies. Mexico isn't one of them, for now.

1) Section 301: the Office of the United States Trade Representative found that practices tied to structural excess capacity in 14 economies, including China, Taiwan, Malaysia and Vietnam, are unreasonable and burden or restrict United States commerce. Proposed tariffs go up to 15% for Taiwan, 18% for Malaysia and 35% for Vietnam. These are proposed "up to" rates, net of some existing duties, with some goods exempt. Nothing is final: written comments are due January 5, 2027, and hearings start January 25, 2027. The Trade Representative hasn't made determinations on Mexico or Norway at this time.

2) Nvidia: the Financial Times reports, as carried by Reuters, that Nvidia told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers with its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. It follows new United States license rules for advanced chips that took effect last week. It's not clear if the halt is temporary. Nvidia, Dell and Supermicro didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

3) FC-BGA substrates: industry sources told The Electronic Times that some FC-BGA substrate processing equipment now takes about 30 months to arrive, up from about six months. Not confirmed: the paper didn't name its sources.

My read: no decision on Mexico helps the nearshoring case, but Mexico's case is still open.

Who it affects: buyers sourcing from Asia can model the proposed rates and watch the January dates. Sellers of AI servers into Southeast Asia should check license status with their partners. Design engineers working with advanced packages can keep an eye on substrate lead times.

The biggest growth engine in my business this year wasn't a marketing strategy.

It was people.

(Writing this while quietly going through the 300 messages in my inbox. I promise I'll get through them all!)

The people I met, the rooms I walked into, the places I had the courage to enter alone, the conversations that turned into collaborations and the random coworking sessions in unexpected places.

A few months ago, someone asked me what advice I'd give to someone growing their own business. My answer? Put yourself out there. Invite people for coffee (digital coffee counts), go to more events and actually talk to people. Ironically, advice I wasn't following myself at the time.

At Web Summit, I heard some of the most successful startup founders sharing exactly this approach to growth: talk to your customers constantly, especially your first 100, and never stop reaching out.

Something I've been putting into practice while speaking with 70+ people for the new travel tech venture I'm collaborating on.

But enough theory. Here's some evidence of my slightly unhinged people moments:
🇬🇧 Sarah Lonorgan— A week in the UK for what I called our Personal Brand Hackathon. A week of exchanging ideas, challenging each other and figuring things out.

🐔 Bella Anastasiou — My growth engineering partner in crime. Coworking sessions, chickens and constant conversations that challenge the way I think about context engineering.

🎲The Bansko crew — Creatives, engineers, big ideas and enough board games to question whether we were actually there to work. Fun fact: one of these conversations even sparked the idea of buying a house.

🌴Martí Panés& Mila Dyankova— My creative partners in crime. Coworking in Indonesia, sharing ideas, helping each other and finding the courage to start building my own thing.

And a bonus mention to Goncalo Hall and Chantelle Flores for an endless week of networking and conversations during Web Summit that opened up some great opportunities for my ventures.

Different places, different people, different conversations. But always the same ingredients: sharing, building, challenging ideas and making things happen.

Looking back, some of my client relationships came directly from these moments. Not from a perfectly planned sales funnel or cold outreach sequence, but from showing up, sharing what I do and finding genuine ways to collaborate.

I think we sometimes overcomplicate growth. (Hot take, I know.)

I LOVE a good strategy, but sometimes the best growth opportunity starts by putting yourself in the right room and meeting people who make you think differently.

If there's one thing I'm taking from this year:
Put yourself out there. Share what you're building. Be curious. Say yes to the coffee.
You never know where a conversation might lead.

Sometimes it's a new client, a new venture, a new idea... or a coworking session with chickens. 🐔

posts.text:
16 miners dead. 10 still missing. And the rain wasn't the surprise.

On Monday night, the Ciseureuh River in West Java overflowed into a ~100 m illegal gold mine shaft in Bogor.

Headlines say "heavy rain." But:

▸ Bogor is one of the wettest places in Indonesia
▸ November is the start of the rainy season
▸ A river next to an open shaft is a known risk

This wasn't an unforecastable extreme. It was a seasonal hazard meeting zero protection.

What a water engineer sees:

▸ No flood bund between river and shaft
▸ No pumping capacity, no level alarm, no evacuation trigger
▸ ~16 hours before the alarm reached police, because illegal sites don't call for help...
▸ A systemic problem: 1,400+ illegal gold mines counted in Indonesia, fewer than 100 closed

The lesson:

▸ Flood risk isn't only about rainfall
▸ It's about where water meets people with no barrier, no data and no voice
▸ Early warning fails if the people most at risk sit outside every system it's built for

Our thoughts are with the families and the 325 rescuers still working in the dark.

WHEN THE CHIPS STOP COMING

Today’s news should be a wake-up call.

NVIDIA has reportedly told manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

For a country that has attracted billions into data centres and AI infrastructure, the immediate reaction may be:

What happens now?

My answer:
DO NOT PANIC. MOVE UP THE VALUE CHAIN.

This moment exposes something important.

We can build the data centres.
We can supply the land.
We can generate the power.
We can provide the cooling.
We can install the fibre.

But if somebody else controls the most critical technology inside those buildings—
somebody else still controls the switch.

That is the lesson.

So what should Malaysia do now?

First, become one of the world’s most trusted AI-compute jurisdictions.

Strong compliance.
Clear end-user verification.
Traceable hardware.
Auditable data centres.
Zero tolerance for diversion.

Make Malaysia the country where global technology companies know their technology is safe.

Second, diversify.

Do not build an entire national AI strategy around one company, one chip or one architecture.
Develop multiple lawful compute pathways.
Build resilience into the ecosystem.

Third—and most importantly—
OWN MORE OF THE INTELLIGENCE.

Our ambition cannot stop at hosting servers.

Build Malaysian AI companies.
Build models.
Build applications.
Build sensors.
Build robotics.
Build semiconductor IP.
Build algorithms.
Build patents.
Build technologies the rest of the world eventually needs.

Because the highest-value layer is rarely the concrete building containing the machines.
It is the intellectual property running through them.

Malaysia has spent years attracting the infrastructure.

Good.

Keep building it.

But now this news reminds us why the next phase matters even more.

FROM HOSTING COMPUTE TO CREATING INTELLIGENCE.

The data-centre boom was never supposed to be the final destination.
It was the platform.

Now Malaysian founders, universities, engineers, scientists and investors must use that platform to create what we actually own.

Our IP.
Our companies.
Our technology.
Our human capital.
Our inventions.

This setback may even become an opportunity.

Because constraints force countries to ask harder questions.

What are we dependent on?
What can we build ourselves?
Where can we create leverage?
What can Malaysia own that nobody can simply switch off tomorrow?

That is where the next game begins.

HOST THE COMPUTE.
BUILD THE CAPABILITY.
OWN THE IP.

And remember this:
If someone else controls the chips, they can control the switch.

So build the things nobody else can switch off—
OUR IDEAS.
OUR INVENTIONS.
OUR INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY.

That is how Malaysia turns an AI infrastructure boom into lasting national power.🚀

Law has Harvey. Finance has its own AI. Piping and Pipeline Engineering still has none.

After 35+ years in Oil & Gas, across Indonesia, the Gulf and the UK, I keep seeing the same gaps:

🔸 Knowledge walks out the door. Senior engineers retire, and their experience leaves with them. What they knew about pump suction layout, nozzle loads or load case selection was never fully written down.
🔸 Juniors learn by trial and error. Many first CAESAR II models get built by copying someone else's file, not by understanding why.
🔸 The answers are scattered. ASME codes, company standards, project specs and design bases all say slightly different things, and finding the right clause takes hours.
🔸 General AI isn't safe for this. Ask a chatbot for an allowable stress or a flange rating and it may give you a confident number that is simply wrong. In our work, that is not a small error.

So at PipingPro Academy we're planning a Vertical AI Agent built only for piping and pipeline engineering, which would:

✅ Guide you through stress analysis step by step, from collecting data to the final report
✅ Use only verified code and material data, and say "not in my database" instead of guessing
✅ Share layout, support and material know-how from real EPC projects

The hard part isn't the AI. It's the trust:
• Every value must be traceable to a code or source
• Client and project data must stay confidential
• The engineer must stay responsible, and the agent must support judgement, not replace it

So I'd value your view:
👉 Where does your team lose the most engineering hours?
👉 What would an AI agent need to prove before you trusted it?

🌍 **From Waste Gas to Nutritious Food: Scientists Just Cracked the Code on CO2-to-Protein Conversion** 🧬

What if we could turn the carbon dioxide that's warming our planet into a delicious, protein-packed food? Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis just made it reality. 🚀

**The Breakthrough**
A team of engineers led by Joshua Yuan has developed an innovative electro-biomanufacturing platform that converts waste CO2 directly into edible protein using artificial photosynthesis. They designed a clever copper-gold tandem catalyst that transforms CO2 into intermediate molecules that a fast-growing edible fungus called *Neurospora intermedia* can consume and convert into nutrient-dense biomass.

**Why This Matters**
The numbers are genuinely mind-blowing. 📊 The resulting fungal biomass contains **48.5% protein**—substantially higher than beef (20.4%) or soy (36%). But here's where it gets really exciting:

✅ **Production speed:** Just 7 days to grow, compared to 645 days for beef and 122 days for soy
✅ **Water efficiency:** Only 794 liters per kilogram of protein, versus 75,600 liters for beef and 5,970 liters for soy
✅ **Land productivity:** 22 times more protein per unit of land than soybeans, and 513 times more than beef
✅ **Sustainability:** Powered by renewable electricity, the process could achieve net-negative greenhouse gas emissions
✅ **Nutrition:** Beyond protein, the biomass contains beta carotene, B vitamins, and heart-healthy unsaturated fatty acids

**The Real-World Impact**
With the UN projecting we'll need nearly 50% more agricultural production by 2050, conventional farming simply can't keep up. This technology offers a scalable alternative that uses minimal resources and could operate at just $3–5 per kilogram of biomass.

The fungus used in this research is already used to make oncom, a traditional fermented food in Indonesia, and is similar to fungus-based meat alternatives already available in U.S. markets.

**What's Next?**
Yuan's lab is now working to scale up production and commercialize this process as an affordable, high-protein alternative for addressing food deserts, supporting space missions, and strengthening national food security.

**What do you think? Would you try a protein product made from CO2? How do you see this technology fitting into the future of sustainable food systems?** 💭

Two seemingly unrelated stories from the past week taught software engineers the exact same lesson:
1. An Anthropic mathematician (Levent Alpöge) published a 17-million-line Lean proof of the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis created with Claude. The Lean & Mathlib community certified the machine-checked proof as valid (though the human-readable proof hasn't been published yet).
2. Together AI disclosed that one of its own AI coding agents accidentally committed a credential to a public GitHub repo. Even after the commit was reverted, an attacker grabbed it and downloaded customer prompt samples.
The takeaway?
Nobody can manually read 17 million lines of code to "trust" AI. Mathematicians trust the Riemann proof because an independent kernel (Lean) verified every step. In production software, eyeballs aren't enough either—you need type-checkers, automated tests, pre-commit/CI secret scanning, and short-lived credentials.

Here are the 5 biggest stories from AI Weekly – Week 47 (Nov 16–23):
🔹 Anthropic goes public on Nasdaq (ANT)
Priced at $83/share for an ~$81B offering—surpassing SpaceX's $75B IPO in June (per Fox Business & CBS News)—and closed up ~17% on day one (per Forbes). For builders, the real signal starts next quarter, when Claude's revenue and compute costs become public on a regular cadence.
🔹 Nvidia's 11 days without Jensen Huang

During a recent field trip to Indonesia, I saw a track maintenance team using standard handheld angle grinders to cut heavy steel rails. 🛠️🚆
While versatile on standard metal, cutting heavy rail steel (like U71Mn or R260) with un-clamped handheld tools raises a vital technical question: How do we maintain structural integrity and safety under extreme friction?

Cutting rails isn't just about speed—it’s about preserving rail end quality for post-welding and protecting the operator. 3 critical factors to consider:
1️⃣ Lateral Impact Resistance: Handheld cutting generates severe lateral wobble. Multi-layer high-tensile fiberglass mesh isn't optional—it’s the core safety net.
2️⃣Cool Cutting & Thermal Control: Self-sharpening grains (like ceramic alumina) prevent excessive heat buildup, eliminating micro-cracking and heat-affected zones (HAZ).
3️⃣High Cut-Yield Speed: Completing a single heavy rail cut in ~60 seconds minimizes track possession time and operator fatigue.

Equipment realities vary by market, but rail safety compliance remains universal.
❓To the railway engineers, track supervisors, and MRO distributors in my network:
From your perspective as a rail industry professional—what truly makes a rail cutting disc a "good product"? Is it pure cutting speed, safety margins, or cost per cut?
I’d love to read your field insights in the comments! 👇

Recently, I built a web app (https://lnkd.in/gbHj_ZnN) using 25 years (2001–2026) of LANCE-processed 1 km MODIS active fire data (via FIRMS on Google Earth Engine (GEE)) to benchmark hotspot activity across Sumatra, Kalimantan, and Papua—drilling down from Province to Kecamatan level against local historical baselines.

Yesterday, I attended Webinar BRIGHTS Series #5 hosted by BRIN’s Research Center for Geoinformatics: "Prediksi Kebakaran Lahan Gambut Berbasis Citra Satelit: dari Pemantauan hingga Peringatan Dini." Following Prof. Parwati Sofan’s presentation on smart satellite monitoring—moving from smoldering peat detection (using MODIS and finer 375 m VIIRS) toward prediction and early warning—reinforced a reality every geospatial engineer has to face: the distance between raw satellite radiance and validated peatland fire mapping is still wide. Even a consistent 25-year 1 km MODIS Near Real-Time record carries real physical trade-offs compared to finer-resolution sensors and science-quality archives.

Working within the constraints of a downstream LANCE/MODIS product, I focused on three physics-aware revisions rather than plotting raw counts blindly:

1. Confidence-Level Filtering
Stripping out low-confidence thermal noise (sun glint, hot bare surfaces) to clean up administrative rankings—while keeping the precision vs. recall trade-off visible, since thick smoke over smoldering peat can depress confidence scores.

2. T21 Brightness Temperature Filtering
Using the 4 µm mid-infrared channel (T21) to separate high-intensity flaming signatures from weak thermal anomalies—recognizing that T21 captures combustion intensity rather than fuel type alone, since smoldering peat burns cooler than flaming fronts.

3. A Persistence Proxy ("Peat Persist")
Calculating Total Detections ÷ Unique Active 1.1 km Grid Cells. A fast-moving grassland or mineral-soil fire clears a 1.1 km footprint in one or two overpasses. Deep peat smolders in the exact same grid cell for days or weeks, driving that repeat ratio sharply upward.

Even with these revisions, Prof. Parwati’s work is a grounded reminder to stay honest about what remains a proxy: repeat-detection ratios can still be skewed by static industrial flares unless masked against peatland boundaries, and cooler subsurface smoldering beneath dense haze still evades coarse 1 km thermal sensors.

Grateful to Badan Riset dan Inovasi Nasional RI (BRIN RI) and Prof.Parwati Sofan for sharing such deep work on tropical peatland fire detection. For EO practitioners working with MODIS/VIIRS fire products: how do you balance false-positive filtering against losing cooler smoldering detections?

🎙️ At 32, one step from Partner at McKinsey, Mickael Roger resigned on a Thursday. By Monday morning he was alone on his couch asking himself, "What are you going to do?" 

The answer came from a bad property call years earlier: he bought in Bondi on advice when his own model said the Gold Coast.
  
In this episode of Strategy Bites, I chat with Mickael, Co-Founder of PropHero, an AI-driven property investment platform now operating across Australia, Spain, Indonesia and Ireland. 

Mickael's path has taken him from engineering and investment banking at UBS to Roland Berger and McKinsey, where he was an Associate Partner.

In this episode:
➡️ The 20-year plan he wrote at 16, and how he followed it
➡️ Flying to Africa alone at 21 to negotiate an M&A deal at Roland Berger
➡️ Roland Berger vs McKinsey: culture, clients and the power of the network
➡️ Building an AI commodity forecasting tool that outperformed a room of traders
➡️ The golden handcuffs: stay for Partner, go corporate, or build your own
➡️ Why he saved a year of expenses before leaving
➡️ The one question to ask before you build anything: "Would you pay for it?"
➡️ Why going "one foot in" kills your chances as a founder
➡️ Taking PropHero global before it had money in the bank
➡️ What goes wrong when you enter a new market, and why you should "trust and check"
➡️ Building a startup in Australia vs overseas
➡️ What he looks for when hiring ex-consultants, and the best role to take if you want to found a business one day

If you're weighing up your own career crossroads, share this episode with someone who needs it.

posts.text:
One thing I genuinely enjoy about software development is taking an idea and turning it into something people can actually use. 

That's what I set out to do with Nath ResellDesk.

ResellDesk is a ticket reseller management application I built to make everyday business activities easier. It helps users manage ticket inventory, record sales, monitor revenue and profit, track events, and receive notifications.

Building this project involved more than writing code. I worked on the interface, authentication, browser-based data storage, serverless functions, email delivery, notification integrations, deployment, and debugging.

Here is the actual technology stack behind ResellDesk:

🔹 Frontend

- HTML5
- CSS3 (CSS Variables, Grid, Flexbox and Media Queries)
- Vanilla JavaScript (ES Modules)
- Google Fonts (DM Sans and Plus Jakarta Sans)
- Browser APIs (IndexedDB, localStorage, Fetch API and HTML Dialog)

🔹 Authentication

- Supabase Auth
- supabase-js 2.45.4

🔹 Data Storage

- IndexedDB (ResellDeskDB) for locally storing tickets and sales records in each user's browser
- localStorage for saving theme preferences

🔹 Backend and Notifications

- Netlify Functions
- Node.js
- esbuild
- Resend for email delivery
- Telegram Bot API
- Discord Webhooks

🔹 Hosting and Deployment

- Netlify
- GitHub
- Netlify Environment Variables
- Automatic deployment from GitHub

🔹 Development Tools

- Visual Studio Code
- Git
- GitHub
- Netlify CLI
- "netlify dev" for local development and testing

A few technical details worth mentioning:

ResellDesk uses Vanilla JavaScript. There is no React, no frontend framework and no build step.

Supabase handles authentication, while IndexedDB stores ticket and sales records locally in each user's browser. Cloud synchronisation is not currently implemented.

Netlify hosts the application and serverless notification function, while Resend handles email delivery through a verified domain. Telegram and Discord are used for administrator alerts.

I'm sharing this project because I want people to see not just the finished application, but also the technologies, engineering decisions and practical development skills behind it.

I'm constantly learning, building and improving my craft as a Full-Stack Software Engineer.

Would you like to see Nath ResellDesk in action?

I've placed the live project link in the comments. Visit it, explore the application and let me know what you think. Your feedback would mean a lot! 🙌

From Spring Boot to FastAPI: A Java Architect’s Journey into AI Engineering

After 12 years of building enterprise applications with Java, Spring Boot, microservices and cloud technologies, I have recently been exploring the Python ecosystem for Generative AI and AI-native application development.

Two technologies that particularly caught my attention are FastAPI and Pydantic.

What I find fascinating is how familiar the underlying engineering principles are:

🔹 Java DTOs → Pydantic Models

🔹 Jakarta Bean Validation → Pydantic Validation

🔹 Spring REST Controllers → FastAPI Endpoints

🔹 Spring Dependency Injection → FastAPI Depends

🔹 OpenAPI Contracts → Schema-driven AI Workflows

The programming language changes. The architectural principles remain relevant.

However, in AI-powered applications, these technologies serve an even more interesting purpose.

FastAPI enables us to expose LLMs, RAG pipelines and AI agents as enterprise-ready API services.

Pydantic helps establish structured data contracts between probabilistic LLMs and deterministic software systems.

Together, they provide a foundation for building reliable, scalable and maintainable AI-powered microservices.

As part of my ongoing learning journey, I am currently exploring Pydantic for LLM Workflows through DeepLearning.AI and connecting these concepts with my existing enterprise architecture experience.

For experienced software professionals transitioning into AI, I believe the opportunity is not necessarily in replacing our existing expertise but in extending it.

Java taught me how to engineer distributed systems. Python is opening new possibilities for integrating intelligence into those systems.

The next milestone: designing and implementing AI-native microservices that integrate seamlessly with existing enterprise platforms.

Looking forward to sharing more practical implementations and architectural insights.

posts.text:
"Can an Indonesian actually own property in Dubai?"

I get this question a lot from Indonesian families, both in Jakarta and in Singapore. Short answer: yes, outright.

A few things people are surprised by:

• Foreigners can buy freehold in Dubai's designated freehold areas, which cover most of the places people actually want to live or rent out.
• You don't need to live in the UAE or hold residency to buy.
• The title deed is issued by the Dubai Land Department, in your own name or a company's.
• When you buy off-plan, your payments go into a regulated escrow account, not straight to the developer.
• Abu Dhabi has opened up too. Foreigners can now own freehold in its investment zones.

The bigger questions are usually how to hold it (personal name, company or family structure) and how it passes to the next generation. That's where a bit of planning up front saves a lot later.

Curious what others have found. What surprised you most when you first looked at buying abroad?

🚀 INTRODUCTION TO JEE (JAKARTA EE) – ENTERPRISE JAVA DEVELOPMENT
After understanding Core Java, JDBC, and Design Patterns, let's move towards building enterprise-level Java applications!
🔹 What is JEE?
JEE (Java Enterprise Edition), now known as Jakarta EE, is a platform built on Java for developing large-scale, secure, distributed, and web-based enterprise applications.
It provides a collection of APIs, specifications, and services that help developers build scalable and maintainable applications.
🔹 Why Do We Need JEE?
Core Java helps us develop standalone applications, and JDBC allows us to connect Java applications with databases.
But enterprise applications require much more, such as:
Handling multiple users and requests.
Managing user sessions.
Building dynamic web applications.
Implementing security and authentication.
Managing business logic and transactions.
Developing scalable applications.
JEE provides technologies to handle these requirements.
🔹 Important Technologies in JEE
Here are some important technologies used in enterprise Java development:
Servlets – Handle client requests and generate responses.
JSP (JavaServer Pages) – Create dynamic web pages.
JDBC – Connect Java applications with databases.
JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) – Manage database persistence using Java objects.
EJB (Enterprise JavaBeans) – Support enterprise business components.
JAX-RS – Develop RESTful web services.
JMS (Jakarta Messaging) – Support message-based communication.
Jakarta Security – Handle authentication and authorization.
🔹 How Does JEE Work?
A typical enterprise web application follows this flow:
Client → Web Server / Servlet Container → Java Application → Database → Response to Client
🔹 Where Is JEE Used?
Banking applications
E-commerce platforms
Enterprise management systems
Insurance applications
Large-scale business applications
🔹 JEE vs Core Java
Core JavaJEE / Jakarta EEGeneral-purpose Java developmentEnterprise application developmentStandalone applicationsWeb and enterprise applicationsBasic Java APIsEnterprise APIs and specificationsJava SE platformBuilt on Java SE
🔹 What Will We Learn Next?
In this series, we will explore:
Servlets and Servlet Architecture
Servlet Lifecycle
Request and Response Handling
Session Management
JSP Concepts and Lifecycle
MVC Architecture
💡 Key Takeaway:
JEE extends Java development beyond standalone applications and provides technologies for building enterprise-level applications.
Let's begin our journey into Enterprise Java Development!
